beats.narration_text: Last time: a neural net is simple parts, and nobody writes its weights. This is Sai. Part two of Stephen Wolfram's tour of what's inside ChatGPT: what you actually see when you open a trained net, from a vision net to GPT-2 itself.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hello, Sai'
'what they encode: quite unknown' lands last and holds

props.command: Part two. A neural net is simple parts with learned weights. Now open a trained one: what do its layers and weights actually show, and what can we read from them?
output: layer 1 of a vision net: things we can name

beats.narration_text: So what does looking inside show? Feed a cat picture to a net trained to tell cats from dogs. In its first layer, you can still name some of what you see: the cat without its background, the outline of the cat. By the tenth layer, Wolfram writes, it's harder to interpret. The net is picking out features, maybe pointy ears, but mostly ones we have no names for.

show.event: the first layer's images of the cat are up first
the tenth layer's unreadable images join them

panels.caption: Layer 1: the cat without its background, its outline

beats.narration_text: Now the language side. ChatGPT itself can't be downloaded, but GPT-2, the small model Wolfram uses for his examples, can. We opened its weights file on this Mac: twelve attention blocks, twelve heads in each, seven hundred sixty-eight numbers per token, a hundred twenty-four million weights. Our rerun even matches his first figure's next-word odds, to the decimal.

props.title: GPT-2, opened on this Mac
props.note: Tensor shapes in openai-community/gpt2 model.safetensors (124,439,808 weights; heads from config.json) · evidence/gpt2_inspect.py, 25 Oct 2026

beats.narration_text: Where does that number come from? Count the shapes. The token table: about fifty thousand tokens, seven hundred sixty-eight numbers each. Then each block: twelve d squared plus thirteen d, about seven million. Twelve blocks, plus the table of positions, add up to exactly one hundred twenty-four million, four hundred thirty-nine thousand, eight hundred eight. Every weight is accounted for.

show.event: the total, as a sum of shapes, typesets

props.title: Where GPT-2's weights are
props.note: Every weight accounted for, none of them explained.
props.conditions: V = 50,257 tokens · P = 1,024 positions · d = 768 · L = 12 blocks. Per block: attention 4d² + feed-forward 8d², plus 13d biases and scales. Tensor shapes: evidence/gpt2_inspect.py.

beats.narration_text: Inside, each word becomes a list of numbers. Projected flat, words with related meanings land near each other: alligator beside crocodile. In the first block of GPT-2, twelve attention heads look back over the text, each with its own pattern. Here's one of its weight matrices, seven hundred sixty-eight by seven hundred sixty-eight. It looks like static. Smooth it, and some structure appears. What that structure encodes, Wolfram writes, is quite unknown.

show.event: the word map is up first, alligator beside crocodile
its smoothed version arrives beside it

beats.narration_text: So, part two: in GPT-2 you can print every one of a hundred twenty-four million numbers, and say exactly where each one sits. What no one can do yet is read them. Wolfram calls ChatGPT's success a scientific discovery, an honest way of saying nobody has a theory for why it works.

show.event: the GPT-2 and accounting lines fill in

props.artifactHeading: What looking inside shows · one page
artifactLines: Early layers of a trained vision net show things we can name. By the tenth layer, mostly not.
GPT-2 opens on a laptop: 12 blocks, 12 heads, 768 numbers per token, 124,439,808 weights.
Every weight is accounted for: 12d² + 13d per block, plus the token and position tables.
Seeing every weight is not reading them. Wolfram calls the success a scientific discovery, with no theory yet.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. GPT-2 is free and runs on a laptop. Load it, count its weights, and plot one of its weight matrices. Then ask an assistant the hard question: what does that picture actually tell you about what the model knows, and what can't it tell you? Then check its answer against the picture.
